newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS-KLM discusses state share buy-back.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-KLM discusses state share buy-back.

text.p: Dutch carrier KLM said on Monday it was in exploratory talks with the Dutch government on the possible buy-back of state-owned KLM shares, rekindling hopes of a link-up with British Airways.

"The State of the Netherlands and KLM confirm that they are conducting exploratory talks on a possible partial sale of KLM shares by the state," KLM and the government said in a four-line joint statement.
"The talks are still at such an early stage that it would be premature to predict whether these talks will eventually lead to a sale of KLM shares by the state," the statement said.
KLM shares, pressured recently by poor first-half operating profits, climbed 3.90 guilders to 45.50 on the news, later settling at 45.30 guilders or nine percent up on the day.
Dutch analysts and dealers said the talks were seen by the market as a step in the right direction towards making KLM a more attractive alliance partner.
"KLM is currently in rather an ambiguous position, regarded by some as a semi-government institution," said Corne Zandbergen, airlines analyst with Generale Bank.
The government currently owns a 38.2 percent voting interest in KLM, made up of 25.7 million common shares, 11.8 million "A" cumulative preference shares and 1,300 priority shares.
A reduction of the government's stake would make it more attractive to non-state-owned airlines, Zandbergen said.
Gilissen's Frits de Vries agreed. "That's undoubtedly one of the reasons why they (KLM) have embarked on these talks," he said, adding "rumour has it they are still negotiating with British Airways."

Merger speculation has repeatedly linked KLM with British Airways, although British Airways' proposed partnership with U.S. giant American Airlines has cast doubts on the likelihood of such an alliance.

Dutch daily newspaper De Telegraaf said on Monday that the state sell-off was part of a plan to overhaul KLM's ownership structure in such a way as to strengthen the Dutch hand in top-secret negotiations on a three-way KLM-BA-AA link-up.
But analyst Gert Jochems of NIB Strating said prospects of a three-way alliance were extremely remote: "KLM has nothing to add to a British Airways-American Airlines partnership."
A buy-back of state-owned shares would however give a much-needed boost to shareholder value, he said, adding: "It's a nice gesture."
KLM spokesman Peter Wellhuner declined to elaborate on Monday's company statement, saying it would be premature to give details.
"KLM has repeatedly stated that one of the options is the buy-back of its own shares, given its ample cash position," Wellhuner said.
"The talks are still at an exploratory stage -- of seeing what such a decision would mean," he said. "As such we are not in actual negotiations with the Dutch government."
